reference:
Both come from Rayleigh scattering: air molecules (nitrogen, oxygen) are much smaller than the wavelength of light, and they scatter short wavelengths far more strongly than long ones. The effect goes as 1/wavelength^4, so blue light (~450 nm) is scattered about 5 to 6 times more than red light (~700 nm).

Why the sky is blue: during the day sunlight passes through a relatively short path of air. Blue light is bounced around in all directions, so wherever you look away from the Sun, you see that scattered blue light coming at you. Violet scatters even more, but sunlight contains less violet, some is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are less sensitive to it, so we perceive blue.

Why sunsets are red/orange: when the Sun is near the horizon, its light travels through roughly 10 to 40 times more atmosphere to reach you. Along that long path most of the blue and green is scattered out sideways before it arrives, so the light that comes straight from the Sun is mostly the leftover orange and red. Dust, smoke, pollution and volcanic aerosols add more scattering and can make sunsets even more vivid red.

Bonus: clouds look white because their water droplets are much larger than light wavelengths, so they scatter all colours about equally (Mie scattering).

reference:
An Ethereum address is derived in four steps:

1. Private key: a random 256-bit (32-byte) number, valid if it is between 1 and n-1, where n is the order of the secp256k1 elliptic curve (the same curve Bitcoin uses). Usually written as 64 hex characters.

2. Public key: multiply the curve's generator point G by the private key using elliptic-curve point multiplication: K = k x G. The result is a point (x, y), each 32 bytes. The uncompressed form is 0x04 || x || y (65 bytes); Ethereum drops the 0x04 prefix and uses the 64-byte x||y. This step is one-way: you cannot get k back from K.

3. Hash: compute Keccak-256 of the 64-byte public key. (Note: Ethereum uses original Keccak-256, which differs from the final NIST SHA3-256 in padding.) This gives 32 bytes.

4. Address: take the last 20 bytes (40 hex characters) of that hash and prefix "0x". Example form: 0x5aAeb6053F3E94C9b9A09f33669435E7Ef1BeAed.

Optional checksum (EIP-55): hash the lowercase hex address (without 0x) with Keccak-256; for each letter in the address, capitalise it if the corresponding hex digit of the hash is 8 or higher. Wallets use this mixed case to catch typos.

In practice, wallets usually start from a BIP-39 seed phrase and derive private keys via BIP-32/BIP-44 path m/44'/60'/0'/0/i, then apply the steps above. Contract addresses are different: they come from the deployer address and nonce (CREATE) or a salt and init code (CREATE2).

AC (alternating current) periodically reverses direction: 50 times a second (50 Hz) in Europe, most of Asia, Africa and Australia, and 60 Hz in North America. DC (direct current) flows steadily in one direction, as from a battery, solar panel or USB charger.

Key differences:
- Voltage changes: AC voltage can be stepped up or down easily and cheaply with a transformer (just coils of wire on an iron core). DC conversion needs power electronics.
- Sources: generators at power stations naturally produce AC; batteries, solar cells and fuel cells produce DC.
- Uses: motors, heaters and lights run well on AC; electronics (phones, laptops, LEDs, TVs) need DC internally, which is why they have adapters/power supplies that convert AC to DC.

Why houses use AC:
1. Efficient long-distance transmission: power losses in wires depend on current squared (I^2R). Transformers boost AC to very high voltage (e.g. 110-765 kV) so the current is low and losses are small, then step it down to 230 V or 120 V near your home.
2. Historical: in the 1880s-90s "War of the Currents", Tesla/Westinghouse AC beat Edison's DC because DC could not then be transformed and needed a power plant every mile or so.
3. Simple, robust motors and cheap transformers, and the whole grid and appliance ecosystem is now built around it.

Today high-voltage DC (HVDC) is used for some very long or undersea links, and homes increasingly have DC sources (solar, batteries, EVs) using inverters to connect to the AC grid.

Noise-cancelling headphones function by using built-in microphones to capture ambient sound in real time. This audio data is sent to an internal processor that analyzes the frequency spectrum of the noise. The device then generates an identical but inverted version of this sound wave (negative interference). When this "anti-noise" signal combines with the original noise outside the ear cups, it cancels out the incoming disturbance through destructive interference.
The resulting cancellation occurs primarily at low frequencies where human hearing is most sensitive and noise sources are often generated. While active noise cancellation handles external sounds effectively, passive isolation relies on physical barriers like foam padding and sealed headbands to block high-frequency sounds and prevent leakage.
Limitations include reduced performance in very loud environments or when using headphones over a phone call, as the microphone may pick up background noise instead of the target sound. The effectiveness also depends heavily on proper fit; loose ear cushions allow air to bypass the seal, diminishing the benefit.

Active noise cancelling (ANC) uses microphones and "anti-noise" to cancel sound before it reaches your ear.

How it works:
1. Microphones listen. A feedforward mic on the outside of each earcup picks up outside noise, and a feedback mic inside the cup hears what actually reaches your ear. Most good headphones use both (hybrid ANC).
2. A chip computes the opposite wave. Sound is a pressure wave. The digital signal processor creates a wave with the same amplitude but the opposite phase (shifted 180°): a peak where the noise has a trough.
3. The speaker plays it along with your music. When the noise and the anti-noise meet, they cancel out (destructive interference), so you hear much less of the noise. The feedback mic keeps correcting the result thousands of times a second.

Why it works best on some sounds:
- ANC is most effective on steady, low-frequency sounds such as plane engines, train rumble and air conditioning, because these are predictable and have long wavelengths.
- It is weaker on sudden or high-pitched sounds such as voices, clatter or a baby crying. These are handled mainly by passive isolation: the seal of the ear cushions or ear tips.

That's why fit matters: a poor seal reduces both kinds of noise blocking. "Transparency" mode does the reverse, using the same microphones to pipe outside sound in.

reference:
Your phone's GPS receiver works without mobile data or Wi-Fi because it only listens; it never transmits to the satellites.

How it works:
1. About 31 GPS satellites orbit roughly 20,200 km up, each with very precise atomic clocks. They continuously broadcast radio signals saying "I am satellite X, this is my exact position (orbit data), and this is the exact time I sent this."
2. Your phone receives those signals and measures how long each took to arrive. Since radio travels at the speed of light, delay x speed = distance to that satellite.
3. Trilateration: knowing your distance from several satellites, the phone works out the single point where those spheres intersect. It needs at least four satellites: three for position (latitude, longitude, altitude) and a fourth to correct the error in the phone's cheap clock.
4. Corrections: the system even accounts for relativity (satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds/day fast). Modern phones also use other constellations (Galileo, GLONASS, BeiDou) and often dual-frequency signals for 1-5 m accuracy.

What mobile data adds: "Assisted GPS" downloads satellite orbit data and rough location from the network, so a fix takes a few seconds instead of up to 30 seconds-several minutes for a cold start. Without data, it still works, just slower at first, best outdoors with a clear sky view.

reference:
Gas is the unit that measures the computing work a transaction needs on Ethereum. Every operation costs a fixed amount of gas: a simple ETH transfer uses 21,000 gas, while token swaps or NFT mints use far more. You pay for that gas in ETH, priced in gwei (1 gwei = 0.000000001 ETH). Gas stops spam and infinite loops and pays validators.

Fee = gas used x gas price. Example: 21,000 gas x 2 gwei = 42,000 gwei = 0.000042 ETH.

Before EIP-1559 (London upgrade, August 2021), fees were a blind first-price auction: you guessed a gas price, the highest bidders got in, you often overpaid, and all of it went to miners.

What EIP-1559 changed:
- Base fee: set by the protocol for every block, and burned (destroyed), not paid to validators. It rises up to 12.5% per block when blocks are more than half full and falls when they are less.
- Priority fee (tip): a small extra you add that goes to the validator to include you.
- Max fee: you set a ceiling; you pay base fee + tip and get the difference refunded.
- Flexible block size: blocks target half the gas limit and can stretch to twice the target in bursts (the gas limit was 30 million then and has been raised since).

Result: fees became more predictable and wallets estimate them easily, but EIP-1559 did not make fees cheaper on its own; that came from more block space, layer-2 rollups and blobs (EIP-4844). Burning the base fee also reduces ETH supply, which can make ETH net deflationary when the network is busy.

Every year, rangers in Rocky Mountain National Park treat countless park visitors with headaches, nausea, dizziness, and a host of other ailments. Many of the people they are treating are suffering from Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS), a generic label applied to symptoms commonly experienced by people visiting high altitudes. The people treated by the rangers aren’t all rock climbers and mountaineers. Many of them are simply enjoying an easy hike or leisurely drive through the park with their family or friends. When travelling above 8,000 feet, everyone is susceptible to AMS.

As a person ascends through the atmosphere, every breath contains fewer and fewer molecules of oxygen. The body’s efforts to compensate for the reduced atmospheric pressure and a lower concentration of oxygen result in the symptoms associated with AMS. In order to avoid worsening symptoms, learn to recognize early signs of AMS.

Symptoms of mild AMS include mild headaches, increased breathing, rapid pulse, nausea, loss of appetite, lack of energy, and general malaise. These are warning signs not to go any higher than you already are.

A person suffering from moderate AMS may begin vomiting, experiencing increased shortness of breath and a headache that doesn’t respond to typical pain relievers. If you or someone you are travelling with experience these symptoms, it is important to descend to lower elevations immediately. Spend at least a day at an elevation where you are comfortable before attempting to ascend again.

If symptoms advance to a lack of balance or coordination, slurring of words, altered mental state, extreme shortness of breathe, a wet or rasping cough, or blue skin, the person may be experiencing severe AMS and their life may be in jeopardy. Go down immediately and seek medical attention.

The easiest way to treat AMS is to prevent it. Remember these simple rules when travelling to altitude. When travelling to high altitude (above 10,000 feet), it is wise to spend at least one night at a moderate elevation before ascending. Climb as high as you like during the day but never spend the night more than 1,000 feet higher than the night before. Remember that if you’re thirsty, you’re already dehydrated. Drink water often. Never take a headache with you when ascending. Treat the headache before going any higher. If you can’t treat it, you’re already too high.

question: What's the difference between a hurricane, a typhoon and a cyclone?
field_atlas_1_4_1: A hurricane is a specific type of cyclone formed in the Atlantic and Eastern Pacific, whereas a typhoon is a tropical cyclone that forms in the Western Pacific, and a cyclone is the general term for any low pressure system with spiraling winds [S3].
field_atlas_1_4_2: A hurricane is a specific type of cyclone formed in the Atlantic and Eastern Pacific, whereas a typhoon is a tropical cyclone that forms in the Western Pacific, and a cyclone is the general term for any low pressure system with spiraling winds [S3].

They are the same weather phenomenon: a strong tropical cyclone, a rotating storm system that forms over warm ocean water and has maximum sustained winds of at least 74 mph (119 km/h, 64 knots). The name depends only on where it happens:

- Hurricane: the North Atlantic, Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, and the eastern and central North Pacific (Mexico, Hawaii).
- Typhoon: the Northwest Pacific, west of the International Date Line (Japan, the Philippines, China, Taiwan, Korea, Guam). Very intense ones (150 mph+) are called "super typhoons".
- Cyclone: the South Pacific and Indian Ocean (Australia, Fiji, India, Bangladesh, Madagascar, Mozambique). These are called "severe tropical cyclones" in Australia and "cyclonic storms" or "very severe cyclonic storms" in the North Indian Ocean.

Other differences are regional, not physical:
- Scales: the US uses the Saffir-Simpson category 1–5 scale for hurricanes; Australia and India use their own scales.
- Spin: storms rotate counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
- Seasons: the Atlantic season runs June to November; typhoons occur all year but peak July to October; South Pacific cyclones peak November to April.

Weaker systems are tropical depressions (under 39 mph) or tropical storms (39–73 mph).

question: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon from Earth?
field_atlas_1_4_1: We always see the same side of the Moon from Earth because the Moon takes the same amount of time to rotate around its own axis as it does to revolve around the Earth, a phenomenon caused by tidal forces from Earth that slowed the Moon's rotation [S2][S3].
field_atlas_1_4_2: We always see the same side of the Moon from Earth because the Moon takes the same amount of time to rotate around its own axis as it does to revolve around the Earth, a phenomenon caused by tidal forces from Earth that slowed the Moon's rotation [S2][S3].
reference:
Because the Moon is tidally locked to Earth. It spins once on its own axis in exactly the same time it takes to orbit Earth once, about 27.3 days. As it travels around us, it turns at just the right rate to keep the same face pointed toward Earth.

Why this happened: Earth's gravity pulls harder on the near side of the Moon than on the far side. This stretched the young Moon slightly into an egg shape, with "tidal bulges". When the Moon spun faster than it orbited, Earth's gravity kept tugging on those bulges and acted like a brake. Friction inside the Moon turned that spin energy into heat. Over millions of years, the spin slowed until it matched the orbit. At that point the bulge stays lined up with Earth and the braking stops. Tidal locking is common: most large moons in the Solar System are locked to their planets.

Some details:
- Thanks to libration, a slight wobble caused by the Moon's tilted, elliptical orbit, we actually see about 59% of its surface over time.
- The far side is not the "dark side". It gets just as much sunlight. We just never see it from Earth.
- The same effect is slowly slowing Earth's rotation. The Moon is also moving away from us by about 3.8 cm per year.

Those white lines are contrails (condensation trails), made of ice crystals, not smoke.

How they form: jet engines burn fuel and release hot, humid exhaust containing water vapour plus tiny soot and sulphate particles. At cruising altitude (about 8-12 km) the air is extremely cold, around -40 to -60 °C. The water vapour cools within a second and freezes onto the particles, forming ice crystals: an artificial cloud. It's the same thing as seeing your breath on a cold day.

Why some vanish fast and some linger: it depends on the humidity of the air at the plane's altitude.
- Dry air (below ice saturation): the ice crystals quickly sublimate back into vapour, so the trail is short and disappears in seconds to a minute.
- Humid air (supersaturated with respect to ice): the crystals don't evaporate; they actually grow by taking up moisture from the surrounding air. The trail persists for minutes to hours, spreads out with the wind, and can turn into sheets of cirrus-like cloud covering large parts of the sky.

So a sky full of long-lasting contrails often signals moist upper air, which can be a sign that a weather front and rain is coming. Persistent contrails also matter for climate: they trap heat at night, and their warming effect may be comparable to aviation's CO2. Airlines are testing small altitude changes to avoid these humid layers.

The split happened gradually, for practical reasons, not as a single decision.

1. Too big to govern from one place. The empire ran from Britain to Syria. Messages took weeks, and threats came at the same time on the Rhine and Danube (Germanic peoples) and in the east (the Sasanian Persian Empire). One emperor couldn't be everywhere.
2. The Crisis of the Third Century (235-284). Around 26 emperors in 50 years, constant usurpations, invasions, plague and inflation showed that a single ruler couldn't hold everything together. Generals declared themselves emperor wherever no emperor was present.
3. Diocletian's reforms (284-305). He split rule administratively, first with a co-emperor (286), then the Tetrarchy (293): two senior emperors (East and West) and two juniors, each with their own army and court.
4. Constantine and Constantinople. Constantine reunited the empire but founded Constantinople in 330 as a new capital in the east, closer to the richer, more urban, Greek-speaking provinces and the Persian frontier.
5. Theodosius I (died 395). He was the last emperor to rule both halves. At his death the empire was divided between his sons: Arcadius in the East (Constantinople) and Honorius in the West (Milan, later Ravenna). It was never reunited.

Ethereum switched to proof of stake on 15 September 2022, in an upgrade called "The Merge" (at block 15,537,393, around 06:42 UTC). The original proof-of-work chain merged with the Beacon Chain, a proof-of-stake chain that had been running in parallel since 1 December 2020. Mining ended, and validators who stake 32 ETH now propose and confirm blocks.

Why they did it:
- Energy: proof of stake cut Ethereum's energy use by about 99.95%. It no longer needs huge mining farms, which answered major environmental criticism.
- Lower issuance: new ETH issuance dropped by roughly 90%. Combined with the fee burn added in 2021 (EIP-1559), ETH supply growth fell sharply and at times turned deflationary.
- Security and decentralization: attackers would need to buy and risk large amounts of ETH, which can be slashed for misbehavior. Anyone can take part without specialized hardware, solo or through staking pools.
- Foundation for scaling: it set up later upgrades such as Shanghai/Capella (staking withdrawals, April 2023), Dencun (proto-danksharding, March 2024) and Pectra (May 2025).

Both give you local mobile service; the difference is how you get it.

eSIM: a digital SIM downloaded to your phone via QR code or app (Airalo, Holafly, Nomad, Saily, Ubigi, or local carriers).

Pros: usually the cheapest data, especially for long stays or heavy use; includes a local number for calls, SMS, taxi apps and restaurant bookings; works in any unlocked phone.

- Short trips, multiple countries, or you want data on landing: eSIM.
- Longer stays (2+ weeks in one country), heavy data, or you need a local phone number: local physical SIM (or the local carrier's own eSIM).
- Also check your home carrier's roaming pass; in the EU/UK roaming may already be included.

### What is CPR?

Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is used when a person's heart has stopped beating, called cardiac arrest, or when a person has stopped breathing. CPR is an emergency technique that keeps blood and oxygen moving through the body until emergency medical help arrives.

When someone's heart stops or they stop breathing, every second matters. Without treatment, permanent brain damage can happen quickly. If you know how to perform CPR, you could save a life.

### How is CPR done?

The steps below give you a general overview of CPR. Reading about CPR is not the same as hands-on training. Taking an accredited course is the best way to be prepared in an emergency.

Before starting CPR, check the person. Tap their shoulder and shout, "Are you okay?" Look to see if they are breathing normally. Gasping or gurgling is not normal breathing. If they do not respond and are not breathing normally, start the steps below right away.

Call 911. If someone else is nearby, send them to call while you start CPR.

Send someone to find an AED. An automated external defibrillator (AED) is a device that can shock the heart back into a normal rhythm. It gives you step-by-step voice instructions. AEDs are especially useful in sudden cardiac arrest, when the heart stops unexpectedly due to an electrical problem. AEDs are available in many public places.

Position the person. Make sure that the person is lying on their back. Start CPR right away. Do not wait to move them to a different surface.

Start chest compressions:

- Place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest and place your other hand on top.
- Position your shoulders above your hands, lock your elbows.
- Push straight down, hard and fast to about 2 inches deep.
- Go at a steady pace of about 100 to 120 pushes per minute.
- Let the chest fully rise back up between each push.

If you haven't had any CPR training, you can do hands-only CPR for a teen or adult whose heart has stopped beating. Hands-only CPR uses chest compressions only, with no breaths, to keep blood circulating. Keep pushing until help arrives or the person starts breathing normally.

If you've had CPR training, you can give breaths along with chest compressions. After every 30 compressions:

- Open the airway by tilting the head and lifting the chin.
- Pinch the person's nose shut and give 2 breaths, each lasting about 1 second.
- Watch for the chest to rise.

Use the AED as soon as it is available. Turn the AED on and follow the voice instructions. It will tell you when to stop compressions and when to deliver a shock. Continue CPR right after.

Children need both chest compressions and breaths. Hands-only CPR alone is not recommended for children. Push down about one-third the depth of the child's chest. If an AED has child pads, use them. If not, adult pads may be used.

The steps above are an overview only. To be truly prepared, take an accredited CPR course and refresh your training every two years. Many community organizations, hospitals, the American Heart Association, and the American Red Cross offer classes.

Call emergency services now (or have someone call): in the hotel, shout for staff to call an ambulance and bring the AED (defibrillator); many hotels have one at reception. Put the phone on speaker; the dispatcher will coach you. Common numbers: 911 (US), 112 (Europe and many countries), 999 (UK), 000 (Australia).

Hands-only CPR (adults):
1. Lay him flat on his back on the floor. If he isn't breathing or is only gasping, start CPR immediately.
2. Kneel beside his chest. Put the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest (lower half of the breastbone), the other hand on top, fingers interlocked.
3. Arms straight, shoulders directly over your hands. Push hard and fast: 5-6 cm (2-2.4 in) deep, at 100-120 compressions per minute (the beat of "Stayin' Alive"). Let the chest rise fully between pushes.
4. Don't stop. If you are trained and willing, give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions (tilt head back, lift chin, pinch nose, seal your mouth over his, 1 second each, watch the chest rise). If not, just keep compressing continuously.
5. Swap with another person every 2 minutes if possible, with minimal pause.

When the AED arrives: switch it on and follow its voice prompts. Attach pads to bare chest (one below the right collarbone, one on the left side below the armpit). Stand clear during analysis and shock, then resume compressions immediately.

Keep going until paramedics take over, the AED tells you to stop, or he starts breathing normally (then roll him into the recovery position and monitor).

Sir Tim Berners-Lee, a British computer scientist, invented the World Wide Web while working at CERN, near Geneva.

He proposed it in March 1989 in a document titled "Information Management: A Proposal." His boss Mike Sendall famously wrote "Vague but exciting" on it. A refined version, written with Robert Cailliau, followed in November 1990.

By the end of 1990 he had built the key pieces: HTML, HTTP, URLs, the first web browser/editor (WorldWideWeb) and the first web server, running on a NeXT computer. The first website, info.cern.ch, went live in December 1990, and the web was opened to the public in August 1991. In April 1993, CERN put the software into the public domain, which helped the web spread worldwide.

The web is different from the internet. The internet is the underlying network, dating from the 1970s–80s, and the web is a system of linked pages that runs on top of it.
